interactions.label: A 44-year-old diabetic develops fever and a new lung infiltrate on the fifth day

params.question: A 44-year-old diabetic develops fever and a new lung infiltrate on the fifth day of hospitalisation following knee replacement surgery. Which pathogen group is MOST likely responsible?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: S. pneumoniae dominates in community-acquired pneumonia. After ≥48 hours of hospitalisation, prior antibiotic exposure and prolonged admission favour colonisation by resistant organisms, not typical community pathogens.
Mycoplasma is an atypical community-acquired pathogen causing 'walking pneumonia' in young adults. It would not account for a new infection developing during hospitalisation on day five.

Correct. Pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after admission is hospital-acquired. Prior antibiotic exposure and prolonged hospitalisation allow resistant organisms — Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and MRSA — to colonise the upper airway.
Oral anaerobes are the hallmark of aspiration pneumonia, typically in patients with impaired consciousness or poor dental hygiene — not standard post-operative hospital-acquired infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: The key distinction is the setting. Any pneumonia developing ≥48 hours after hospital admission is classified as hospital-acquired, shifting the likely pathogens to resistant organisms such as Pseudomonas aeruginosa, Acinetobacter baumannii, and MRSA.

Exactly right. Hospital-acquired pneumonia follows ≥48 hours of admission and is dominated by resistant organisms like Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and MRSA, requiring entirely different antibiotic classes than community-acquired pneumonia.

interactions.label: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with progress

params.question: An HIV-positive patient with a CD4 count of 120 cells/mm³ presents with progressive dyspnoea and bilateral interstitial infiltrates on chest X-ray. Which pathogen should be HIGHEST on the differential?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: S. pneumoniae can infect HIV-positive patients at any CD4 level, but the bilateral interstitial pattern and severely depressed CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ point to a specific opportunistic pathogen.

Correct. Below a CD4 count of 200 cells/mm³, Pneumocystis jirovecii — a fungal pathogen — becomes the dominant pulmonary infection in HIV. The bilateral interstitial infiltrate pattern is characteristic of PCP.
Invasive Aspergillus is primarily associated with neutropenia from chemotherapy, not HIV-related immunosuppression. The CD4 count, not the neutrophil count, is the key discriminator in HIV.

CMV pneumonia is primarily a concern in transplant recipients on immunosuppressive therapy. In HIV, the CD4 count below 200 cells/mm³ marks Pneumocystis jirovecii as the signature pulmonary opportunist.

overallFeedback.feedback: In HIV, the CD4 count determines the pathogen spectrum. Below 200 cells/mm³, Pneumocystis jirovecii — a fungal pathogen — is the most likely cause of bilateral interstitial pneumonia. Always match the specific immune defect to its signature pathogen.

Well identified. The CD4 count is the tipping point in HIV: below 200 cells/mm³, Pneumocystis jirovecii takes over as the dominant pulmonary pathogen, requiring specific treatment with co-trimoxazole rather than standard antibacterials.

interactions.label: A 70-year-old man presents with pneumonia. He is confused, his respiratory rate

params.question: A 70-year-old man presents with pneumonia. He is confused, his respiratory rate is 34 breaths per minute, blood pressure is 85/50 mmHg, and serum urea is 9 mmol/L. What is his CURB-65 score?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This significantly underscores the patient. Evaluate each CURB-65 criterion: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure systolic <90 mmHg, and Age ≥65. All five are met here.
Recheck each criterion. Confusion (1), Urea 9 >7 (1), Respiratory rate 34 ≥30 (1), Blood pressure 85/50 with systolic <90 (1), Age 70 ≥65 (1). All five criteria are present.
You may have missed one criterion. All five components of CURB-65 are satisfied: confusion, elevated urea, tachypnoea, hypotension, and age ≥65 years.

Correct. All five CURB-65 criteria are met: Confusion (1), Urea 9 mmol/L which exceeds 7 (1), Respiratory rate 34 which exceeds 30 (1), Blood pressure 85/50 with systolic below 90 (1), and Age 70 which exceeds 65 (1). This mandates ICU-level care.

overallFeedback.feedback: Each letter in CURB-65 awards one point: Confusion, Urea >7 mmol/L, Respiratory rate ≥30/min, Blood pressure (systolic <90 or diastolic ≤60), and Age ≥65. This patient meets all five, scoring 5 — the maximum. A score of ≥2 warrants hospital admission; ≥4 warrants ICU care.

Excellent. A CURB-65 score of 5 places this patient in the highest severity category, mandating ICU admission with broad-spectrum combination antibiotics and consideration for Pseudomonas and MRSA cover.

interactions.label: A 58-year-old woman is admitted with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. The

params.question: A 58-year-old woman is admitted with suspected community-acquired pneumonia. The resident orders intravenous ceftriaxone to be started immediately. Which step is MOST critical to complete before administering the first antibiotic dose?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: HRCT is a second-tier investigation reserved for patients who do not respond to initial treatment or when the diagnosis is uncertain. It should never delay antibiotic therapy.
ABG is indicated when CURB-65 reaches 3 or above, or oxygen saturation falls below 94%. It is important but does not need to precede the first antibiotic dose in every patient.

answers.text: Blood cultures and sputum for Gram stain and culture

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Blood cultures from two separate sites and sputum for Gram stain and culture must be collected before the first antibiotic dose. Post-antibiotic cultures frequently yield false negatives, losing the chance to identify the causative organism.

HIV testing is standard of care per national PITC guidelines and should be performed, but it does not need to precede antibiotic administration. The priority is collecting microbiological samples before the first dose.

overallFeedback.feedback: The cardinal rule is cultures before antibiotics. Blood cultures from two separate sites and sputum for Gram stain and culture must be collected before the first dose. Administering antibiotics first frequently yields false-negative cultures, making targeted de-escalation impossible later.

Precisely. The non-negotiable sequence is cultures and sputum collection first, then the first antibiotic dose. This takes only five to ten minutes and does not delay treatment — but omitting it means losing the microbiological diagnosis.

interactions.label: A patient with community-acquired pneumonia has a CURB-65 score of 3 and is admi

params.question: A patient with community-acquired pneumonia has a CURB-65 score of 3 and is admitted to the medical ward. Which empirical antibiotic regimen is MOST appropriate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Oral amoxicillin is appropriate for outpatient management of CAP with CURB-65 scores of 0–1. A score of 3 requires hospitalisation and intravenous therapy with broader coverage.
Piperacillin-tazobactam is the backbone regimen for hospital-acquired pneumonia, not community-acquired. Matching the antibiotic tier to both the syndrome and severity is critical.

Correct. For hospitalised CAP (CURB-65 score 2–3), IV ceftriaxone covers typical bacterial pathogens while IV azithromycin concentrates inside cells to target atypical organisms that beta-lactams cannot reach.
IV co-amoxiclav is the standard regimen for aspiration pneumonia. For hospitalised CAP, ceftriaxone plus azithromycin provides the necessary dual coverage of typical and atypical pathogens.

overallFeedback.feedback: For hospitalised CAP with CURB-65 of 2–3, the standard regimen is IV ceftriaxone plus IV azithromycin, or IV levofloxacin alone. The combination provides dual coverage: a beta-lactam for typical bacteria and a macrolide for intracellular atypical pathogens. Always match the antibiotic tier to the severity score.

Well chosen. The pharmacology drives this combination: ceftriaxone, a time-dependent beta-lactam, covers typical bacteria, while azithromycin concentrates intracellularly to target atypical pathogens that cephalosporins alone cannot reach. IV levofloxacin alone is an equally valid alternative.

interactions.label: Continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics for the entire treatment course is safer t

params.question: Continuing broad-spectrum antibiotics for the entire treatment course is safer than de-escalating to a narrow-spectrum agent once culture sensitivity results are available.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Broader is not safer. De-escalation at 48–72 hours to the narrowest effective antibiotic based on culture sensitivity is the standard of care. Continuing unnecessary broad-spectrum therapy is, as the video emphasised, the single most preventable management error in pneumonia — it drives C. difficile infection and antimicrobial resistance.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — broader is not safer. At 48–72 hours, culture results should guide de-escalation to the narrowest effective antibiotic. Every extra day of unnecessary broad-spectrum therapy increases the risk of Clostridioides difficile infection and drives antimicrobial resistance.
